q: In The gardener watered the roses, which expression is the whole subject?
e: The complete noun phrase The gardener is the subject; gardener alone is its head, watered is the verb, and the roses is the object.
s: Subjects, predicates and the first sentence patterns

q: In the transparent analysis teach + -er + -s, which part marks plural number?
e: Plural -s is inflectional. Teach is the root, -er forms the person noun, and teacher is the stem receiving the plural ending.
s: Inside words: morphemes, roots, stems and word formation

q: In They will chair the discussion, what is the class of chair?
e: Chair follows modal will as a plain-form lexical verb and selects the discussion as its object.
s: Word classes and the difference between category and function

q: In The parcel was opened by Amina, which statement about the parcel is accurate?
o: It is the agent because every subject is an agent.
It is an adjunct because the clause is passive.
It is the subject and is affected by the opening.
It is the direct object because it is affected.
e: Passive subjects can denote affected participants. Subject is a grammatical function; agent is a semantic role.
s: Subjects, predicates and the first sentence patterns

q: Which expression is a non-finite clause in the analysis used here?
e: To repair contains a non-finite verbal head and its object. The other choices are noun or prepositional phrases.
s: Grammar, meaning and units of structure

q: In a school library, what is the usual analysis of school?
o: a noun functioning as a modifier
an adjective because all modifiers are adjectives
e: A noun may modify another noun without becoming an adjective. School and library are both nouns here.
s: Word classes and the difference between category and function

q: Check the three labelled parts in neutral formal prose: The new assistant [A] / seems [B] / patiently [C]. Choose the faulty part or No error.
e: The intended property of the assistant requires patient, a predicative adjective. The subject and linking verb are well formed.
s: Subjects, predicates and the first sentence patterns

q: Check the labels: The visitors [A] / waited [B] / outside [C]. Choose the faulty part or No error.
e: Waited is intransitive here and outside supplies place. No object is required.
s: Subjects, predicates and the first sentence patterns

q: Which pair illustrates derivation rather than merely two inflections of one lexical item?
e: Kindness is a new noun formed from an adjective; the other pairs supply grammatical forms within the same lexical item.
s: Inside words: morphemes, roots, stems and word formation

q: In The explanation made the audience uneasy, what is uneasy?
e: Uneasy predicates a property of the audience, the direct object of made. It does not name another recipient or participant.
s: Subjects, predicates and the first sentence patterns

q: Which is the established plural of criterion?
e: Criteria is the established ordinary plural. Criterion is singular, criterias adds an inappropriate plural ending, and criterion’s is a genitive form rather than an ordinary plural.
s: Noun meanings and the formation of plurals

q: For ordinary general prose, choose the completed phrase: two useful ____ about the deadline.
e: Information is noncount in this sense; pieces supplies countable units. The other choices misuse number or invent a form.
s: Countability, special number patterns and group agreement

q: Several children share one reading room. Which genitive is correct?
e: Children is an irregular plural, so the genitive adds ’s; no extra plural -s or second apostrophe is needed.
s: Genitives, possession and noun relationships

q: In the phrase the new school library, which word is the noun head?
e: Library is the head; the is a determiner, new an adjective and school a noun modifier.
s: Noun phrases, modifiers, apposition and nominalisation

q: Which statement accurately describes two coffees at a café?
o: Every noncount noun can therefore take two directly.
The numeral turns coffees into a verb.
Coffees is a conventional count use meaning servings.
Coffee can never have a count use.
e: Servings license this count use, but such shifts depend on the noun and context.
s: Countability, special number patterns and group agreement

q: Choose agreement with singular head pair: This pair of scissors ____ new.
e: Pair is the singular head. Scissors alone normally has plural agreement, but does not control this verb.
s: Countability, special number patterns and group agreement

q: Check the labels: The visitors’ coats [A] / were hanging [B] / beside the door [C]. Choose the faulty part or No error.
e: The regular plural visitors forms its genitive with an apostrophe after s; plural coats agrees with were.
s: Genitives, possession and noun relationships

q: Check ordinary informational prose: The adviser offered [A] / several practical advices [B] / before the meeting [C]. Choose the faulty part or No error.
e: Advice is noncount in this sense. Several pieces of practical advice repairs the phrase; the other parts are well formed.
s: Countability, special number patterns and group agreement

q: Which plural correctly marks the head of sister-in-law?
e: Sisters is the head plural in the established compound; law and in do not receive the plural marker.
s: Noun meanings and the formation of plurals

q: Which account of British The team are sharing their separate views is accurate?
o: Plural agreement presents the members individually.
It is ungrammatical in every variety.
Team is always a plural-form noun.
Their proves that team cannot ever take is.
e: British collective agreement can reflect members; singular unit construal is also possible in other contexts.
s: Countability, special number patterns and group agreement

q: Choose the indefinite article by the following sound: She is ____ honest witness.
e: The indefinite article is an because honest begins with a vowel sound. The is definite, and a singular count use of witness needs an appropriate determiner here.
s: Articles, identification and general reference

q: Which explanation fits I bought a particular book yesterday?
o: Only the could refer to a specific purchase.
The noun phrase is indefinite but refers to a specific book.
Indefinite always means no particular book exists.
A makes book a noncount noun.
e: The article does not make specificity impossible; particular and the buying context identify the speaker’s intended specific referent.
s: Articles, identification and general reference

q: Which is the ordinary name of the river in this sentence? We crossed ____.
e: The conventional river name in ordinary reference is the Indus. The alternatives do not give that name in its ordinary use.
s: Articles with institutions, names and abstract nouns

q: Which is the neutral standard phrase?
e: My occupies the central determiner position; it does not combine with a preceding ordinary article in this noun phrase.
s: Determiners, distribution and quantity

q: Complete with an expression meaning a small positive number: We have ____ volunteers, so the event can proceed.
e: A few supplies a positive plural count quantity; a little and much suit noncount nouns, and every requires a singular count phrase.
s: Some, any, few and little: meaning under quantity and negation

q: Which expression excludes every one of the proposals?
e: No excludes all members. Not all excludes complete acceptance but can allow some; some and a few assert acceptance of members.
s: Determiners, distribution and quantity

q: Check the labelled parts in an offer: Would you like [A] / some tea [B] / before we begin [C]? Choose a faulty part or No error.
e: Some is normal in an offer. A rule replacing some with any in every question would reject an established grammatical pattern.
s: Some, any, few and little: meaning under quantity and negation

q: Which phrase illustrates a conventional comparative for separate counted items, rather than a measured noncount amount?
e: Files are counted individual items, so fewer files gives the relevant count comparison. The other phrases are grammatical comparisons of noncount amounts and do not illustrate this count pattern.
s: Some, any, few and little: meaning under quantity and negation

q: Which statement about hospital is accurate?
o: In the hospital cannot describe a patient in standard English.
British and American patient expressions must be identical.
In hospital is a usual British patient pattern; in the hospital is a usual American patient pattern.
Every reference to a hospital must have zero article.
e: Institutional article conventions vary by region and construction; neither standard pattern justifies a universal prohibition.
s: Articles with institutions, names and abstract nouns

q: Which analysis of The violin is difficult to learn is defensible in a general discussion of instruments?
o: The violin can have generic reference to the instrument type.
The always refers to one previously named physical object.
The makes violin a personal pronoun.
Generic statements cannot use the singular.
e: The singular generic construction can present an instrument category; the does not require earlier mention of one physical violin.
s: Articles, identification and general reference

q: Choose the ordinary object form after to in careful edited prose: The invitation was sent to ____.
e: Me is the personal object form; I is subject case, my requires a noun and mine is an independent possessive.
s: Personal forms, case and reflexive meaning

q: Which sentence expresses that Leena herself is the person Leena blamed?
e: Herself expresses the local same-participant object relationship; the distractors misuse subject, possessive or nonstandard apostrophe forms.
s: Personal forms, case and reflexive meaning

q: Choose the pronoun that is subject of will arrive: ____ do you think will arrive first?
e: Who is subject inside will arrive; do you think does not make it an object.
s: Pronoun families and relative choices

q: Which statement about each other and one another is accurate?
o: One another is an ordinary singular personal subject.
Each other must add plural -s after three people.
They normally overlap and can refer to mutual relations among two or more people.
Each other is grammatical only with exactly two.
e: Modern standard use does not enforce the inherited two-versus-more-than-two distinction as a universal rule.
s: Pronoun families and relative choices

q: A person who uses they has arrived. Complete: ____ ready to begin.
e: Singular they retains its usual subject form and are agreement; singular reference does not require they is.
s: Reference chains, agreement and inclusive pronouns

q: In It is raining, what does it do?
o: It fills a dummy subject position.
It must refer to a previously named cloud.
It is the direct object of raining.
e: Weather it need not identify a discourse referent; it occupies the grammatical subject position.
s: Dummy subjects, generic reference and local interpretation

q: Check the standard statement: It is me [A] / who called [B] / about the repair [C]. Choose a faulty part or No error.
e: Object me after be is standard. It is I is a highly formal alternative, not the only grammatical form.
s: Personal forms, case and reflexive meaning

q: Without further context, which problem affects Aisha told Hina that she had won?
o: She must always refer to the nearest noun.
A pronoun cannot occur after that.
She has more than one plausible antecedent.
The sentence lacks a finite verb.
e: Either named person can be the winner in a suitable context, so reference is ambiguous; the structure itself is possible.
s: Reference chains, agreement and inclusive pronouns

q: In Put the file there, which use of there is present?
o: A locative expression identifying a place.
e: There locates the file in this imperative; it differs from existential there introducing a noun phrase.
s: Dummy subjects, generic reference and local interpretation

q: Which reading is ordinary in Before she left, Nida checked the window?
o: She cannot refer forward in any grammatical sentence.
Nida must be the direct object of left.
She can anticipate Nida as its later identification.
e: A forward reference is available in this construction; prior noun mention is not an absolute requirement for pronouns.
s: Reference chains, agreement and inclusive pronouns

q: Which is the past participle of write?
e: Written is the past participle; wrote is past simple, writes a present form and writing the -ing form.
s: Lexical verbs, auxiliaries and the principal forms

q: Complete the ordinary past question: Did the courier ____ on time?
e: Did carries the finite past contrast; the lexical verb is plain arrive.
s: Verb-phrase order, do-support, questions and negation

q: In The panel considered the plan practical, what is practical?
o: An object complement describing the plan.
An indirect object receiving the plan.
A second direct object naming another entity.
e: Practical predicates a property of the object plan; it is not another participant.
s: Valency, objects, predicative complements and sentence patterns

q: Which analysis fits The wax melted?
o: A passive requiring an omitted was.
A clause with wax as direct object.
A sentence without a grammatical subject.
An active intransitive clause with wax as affected subject.
e: The verb occurs in its intransitive alternation; no passive be-participle construction is present.
s: Alternations, dynamic meanings and states

q: Choose the form selected after a core modal: She can ____ the schedule.
e: A core modal normally selects the plain verb form revise.
s: Lexical verbs, auxiliaries and the principal forms

q: Which is the neutral yes–no question corresponding to She is ready?
e: Finite be inverts directly in this neutral question; do-support is not added.
s: Verb-phrase order, do-support, questions and negation

q: Check the labels: Who [A] / wrote the report [B] / yesterday [C]? Choose a faulty part or No error.
e: Who is the subject in an ordinary affirmative subject question; an extra did is not required.
s: Verb-phrase order, do-support, questions and negation

q: Why is The cook is tasting the soup ordinary?
o: Taste has a dynamic action sense in this sentence.
Every sense of taste must use the progressive.
An object always makes a verb stative.
Progressive be can only precede a noun.
e: The cook performs an action, contrasting with stative The soup tastes salty; the spelling alone does not fix the aspectual meaning.
s: Alternations, dynamic meanings and states

q: Which sentence illustrates two noun-phrase objects?
o: The tutor called the learner resourceful.
The tutor gave the learner a booklet.
e: The learner is indirect object and a booklet direct object; resourceful in the last distractor is a predicative complement, not a second object.
s: Valency, objects, predicative complements and sentence patterns

q: In She may have been waiting, which verb is finite?
e: May is the first, finite auxiliary; have is plain after the modal, been a past participle and waiting an -ing form.
s: Lexical verbs, auxiliaries and the principal forms

q: Complete the simple-present negative: This camera ____ store sound.
e: A singular subject takes does; store remains base. The other auxiliaries do not form this simple-present negative.
s: Present simple: tense, time and a speaker’s general view

q: Which verb phrase is present progressive?
e: Present be + -ing makes progressive aspect. Perfect have + participle and simple measures have different structures.
s: Present progressive: activity, temporary patterns and changing states

q: Supply the irregular participle required by perfect have: She has ____ the timetable.
e: Have selects written. Wrote is past simple; writing is an -ing form; write is base.
s: Present perfect: experience, results and time extending to now

q: Which sentence contains a present perfect progressive?
o: The staff have been checking the seals.
The staff are checking the seals.
The staff have checked the seals.
e: Have been checking combines present perfect have with progressive be + -ing. The other forms omit one or both aspects.
s: Present perfect progressive and cumulative application

q: Choose the error, or No error: The printer (A) does not starts (B) automatically (C).
e: Does already carries agreement, so use start. The subject and adverb are well formed.
s: Present simple: tense, time and a speaker’s general view

q: Choose the error, or No error: We (A) are having lunch (B) in the courtyard (C).
e: Have lunch is an activity and permits progressive aspect. There is no possession-sense restriction here.
s: Present progressive: activity, temporary patterns and changing states

q: Which description matches I have known Zara since 2021?
o: One named meeting completed in 2021 only.
A future plan to meet Zara.
A state of acquaintance extending from a past starting point towards now.
A progressive verb form because since appears.
e: Have known is perfect simple, not progressive. Since marks the beginning of a relevant continuing interval.
s: Present perfect: experience, results and time extending to now

q: In Has Omar been waiting?, which word is the finite auxiliary?
e: Has carries present agreement and inverts with the subject. Been and waiting are non-finite verb forms.
s: Present perfect progressive and cumulative application

q: Form a past-simple question: Did the caretaker ____ the gate?
e: Did carries past marking, so lock is base. The other forms duplicate tense/agreement or use an -ing form.
s: Past simple: completed events, states and narrative steps

q: Which phrase is past progressive?
e: Were + -ing forms past progressive; the other choices are perfect or simple past.
s: Past progressive: background, overlap and an unfinished viewpoint

q: Use the participle required by had: The bus had ____ before we reached the stop.
e: Had selects participial gone, not went, going or goes.
s: Past perfect and past perfect progressive: looking back from then

q: Which sentence means that night work is familiar to Sara now?
o: Sara would work nights if asked.
Sara was going to work nights.
Sara is used to working nights.
e: Be used to + -ing means accustomed; the others describe a former habit, a hypothetical response or an earlier intention.
s: Past habits, used to, habitual would and coherent reporting

q: Choose the error, or No error: Who (A) opened the storeroom (B) yesterday (C)?
e: Who is the subject; this affirmative subject question does not require did. All segments are grammatical.
s: Past simple: completed events, states and narrative steps

q: Which construction explicitly foregrounds the duration of activity before a past reference point?
e: Had been + -ing is past perfect progressive. Past progressive gives an internal past view without itself marking anterior duration.
s: Past perfect and past perfect progressive: looking back from then

q: What does They were rebuilding the wall assert on its own?
o: Rebuilding was in progress at the relevant past time.
e: Progressive presents an internal phase. It does not alone assert completion or non-completion of the whole project.
s: Past progressive: background, overlap and an unfinished viewpoint

q: Use the formal edited negative of a former habit: We did not ____ to take that road.
e: After did, the course uses base use in this construction. The -d spelling occurs, but use is the stated formal default.
s: Past habits, used to, habitual would and coherent reporting

q: Which construction is perfect progressive?
e: Has is finite perfect have; been is the participle of be; checking is the progressive -ing form.
s: Combining perfect and progressive viewpoints

q: What does I have been repairing the clock normally leave open without more context?
o: Whether the construction contains a perfect auxiliary
Whether the clock is now completely repaired
Whether the speaker is the subject
e: The construction asserts recent repair activity but does not guarantee completion. The other properties are expressed in the sentence.
s: Combining perfect and progressive viewpoints

q: Which sentence uses have with its ordinary possession meaning?
o: We are having the windows replaced.
e: Have three storage rooms expresses possession; the others describe events or a causative arrangement.
s: States, actions, temporary interpretations and repetition

q: The chef is tasting the sauce. Which analysis is accurate?
o: The sentence asserts that the sauce tastes pleasant.
Is is a perfect auxiliary here.
Tasting describes deliberate sampling, a dynamic interpretation.
e: The chef deliberately samples the sauce; the progressive is natural in this action meaning. No judgement of pleasantness is asserted.
s: States, actions, temporary interpretations and repetition

q: The archive has been closed ____ last Wednesday. Choose the expression that identifies the starting point.
e: Since last Wednesday identifies when the interval began. For needs a duration; during locates within an interval; until gives an endpoint.
s: Duration, starting points and temporal endpoints

q: The archive was closed ____ three weeks and reopened yesterday.
e: For three weeks measures a duration in a completed past situation. For does not require present perfect.
s: Duration, starting points and temporal endpoints

q: Which instruction sets a one-off submission deadline no later than Friday?
o: Wait for the form since Friday.
Submit the form for Friday, meaning the submission began Friday.
e: By Friday supplies the required deadline. Until concerns continuation; the other phrases do not express the stated relationship.
s: Duration, starting points and temporal endpoints

q: Which observation accurately compares common British and American usage for a recent event?
o: British English often uses I have just sent it; American English also commonly uses I just sent it.
American English has no present perfect.
British English always forbids simple past.
e: Both are established; the comparison concerns a frequent regional choice, not the elimination of a tense from either variety.
s: Already, yet, just, lately and recently in context

q: Review for neutral formal English: During the last hour, Mira has been checking the sensors. Which judgement is defensible?
o: Replace checking with checked while keeping all other words.
No error: the perfect progressive naturally presents the recent checking activity.
e: During the last hour is a valid interval; Mira selects has; been checking is an active progressive. None of the proposed changes is required.
s: Combining perfect and progressive viewpoints

q: Which statement gives a reliable distinction between lately and recently?
o: Lately normally frames a recent interval; recently also readily locates a single past event.
Recently requires a progressive in every clause.
Lately means arriving after the scheduled time.
Both words always make a present-perfect answer uniquely necessary.
e: Lately is associated with a recent interval, not lateness. Neither word mechanically selects one tense-aspect construction.
s: Already, yet, just, lately and recently in context

q: Which is a correctly formed will-construction?
o: She will to inspect the roof.
e: Will takes the base form inspect without to or an -s/past ending.
s: Will, shall and be going to: prediction, intention and commitment

q: In Shall we begin?, what is a common British English function of shall?
e: Shall we commonly makes a proposal about joint action; the sentence is not a perfect or past report.
s: Will, shall and be going to: prediction, intention and commitment

q: Which analysis of We are going to review the lease is accurate?
o: The construction can present a prior intention.
Are is an infinitive after a modal.
To review is a destination phrase.
e: Be going to plus a base verb can foreground a prior intention; no physical travel is required.
s: Will, shall and be going to: prediction, intention and commitment

q: The timetable says The ferry departs at 07:20 tomorrow. Which judgement is accurate?
o: The sentence states a repeated event only.
A present-simple schedule can refer to a future event.
Departs must be replaced by will depart.
A present form cannot have future reference.
e: Present simple is established for timetables and future fixed occurrences. No mechanical replacement is required.
s: Present forms for arrangements, timetables and future facts

q: Complete the explicitly requested present-progressive arrangement: We ____ the architect tomorrow.
e: Are meeting is finite be plus -ing, used here for an arrangement; the other sequences are malformed.
s: Present forms for arrangements, timetables and future facts

q: Which construction is future perfect progressive?
e: Will have been waiting combines will, perfect have, participial been and progressive waiting.
s: Future progressive, perfect and perfect progressive

q: Use a future-perfect construction: By Friday, the editor will have ____ all six chapters.
e: Read is the past participle as well as the base spelling of this irregular verb. Have requires the participle here.
s: Future progressive, perfect and perfect progressive

q: Check the intended willingness reading: If you will hold the ladder, I can carry the tools. Which judgement is accurate?
o: No error: will can express willingness in the condition.
Remove will because it is impossible after if.
Replace hold with held while keeping the intended willingness meaning unchanged.
e: Will is not merely a future-time marker here; it means are willing to. The proposed absolute prohibition is false.
s: Future in the past, time clauses and consistent viewpoints

q: Which sentence contains an embedded question about a future arrival time?
o: I will stand up when the guest arrives.
When the guest arrives, we will begin.
We will wait until the guest arrives.
I wonder when the guest will arrive.
e: Wonder selects an embedded interrogative expressing an unknown time; the other subordinate clauses locate main-clause events.
s: Future in the past, time clauses and consistent viewpoints

q: Form the requested normal backshifted report: On Monday she said she ____ on Tuesday. Use would plus leave.
e: Would selects base leave. The task requests a backshifted pattern rather than claiming backshift is obligatory in every reporting context.
s: Future in the past, time clauses and consistent viewpoints

q: The condition of the outer walls ____ deteriorating. Use the ordinary singular head-noun agreement.
e: Singular condition is the subject head; walls belongs to its modifying of-phrase.
s: Person, number and the structure of the subject

q: Which statement correctly describes most ordinary lexical past-tense forms?
o: They add -s for every plural subject.
They do not normally distinguish singular from plural: she arrived / they arrived.
They require a plural participle after every plural noun.
They are all identical to present-tense forms.
e: Most lexical past forms show no number contrast; be is an important exception.
s: Person, number and the structure of the subject

q: For ordinary British English usage, which analysis is accurate?
o: A committee can take singular unit agreement or plural member agreement.
Plural collective agreement proves that the noun is grammatically misspelled.
Collective nouns must always take singular verbs.
Police always takes the same agreement as committee.
e: British English permits unit/member agreement with many collective nouns; the behaviour of individual nouns and varieties needs qualification.
s: Collectives, indefinite pronouns and competing agreement cues

q: Review the intended inclusive statement: Everyone has their own copy. Which judgement is accurate?
o: Their is impossible after a singular antecedent in all standard English.
No error: everyone takes has, while singular their supplies inclusive reference.
Change has to have because their is plural in spelling.
e: The singular finite agreement belongs to everyone. Established singular they/their can supply inclusive personal reference.
s: Collectives, indefinite pronouns and competing agreement cues

q: Choose careful formal existential agreement: There ____ several practical difficulties.
e: The plural postverbal noun phrase takes are in the target formal pattern. Informal there’s with a plural is a separate register-sensitive use.
s: Relative clauses, inversion and existential constructions

q: One of the books that ____ the method is missing. The relative clause explicitly describes the plural group of books.
e: The stated antecedent of that is plural books, so explain is appropriate. Outer one separately takes main-clause is.
s: Relative clauses, inversion and existential constructions

q: Half of the evidence ____ missing.
e: Evidence is a mass noun in this use, so the fraction takes singular is.
s: Quantities, measures, titles and plural-looking forms

q: The number of completed applications ____ risen.
e: The number names a single figure, so has is the ordinary agreement choice. A number of applications have … is a different quantifying construction.
s: Quantities, measures, titles and plural-looking forms

q: Which pair correctly contrasts the discipline with numerical figures?
o: Statistics be demanding; these statistics am incomplete.
Statistics have demanding; these statistics has incomplete.
Statistics is demanding; these statistics are incomplete.
Statistics are demanding as a discipline; these statistics is incomplete.
e: The academic discipline takes singular agreement; the demonstratively identified figures are plural.
s: Quantities, measures, titles and plural-looking forms

q: Which statement about None of the candidates is/are available is most reliable?
o: Only are has ever been standard.
Both singular and plural agreement occur; interpretation and register guidance should be stated.
e: Authorities record both singular and plural agreement with none of a countable set. A context-free absolute prohibition is unreliable.
s: Collectives, indefinite pronouns and competing agreement cues

q: Which analysis of “The room became quiet” is correct?
o: quiet is an adverb modifying became
quiet is an adjective functioning as subject complement
e: Became is a linking verb here. Quiet characterises room; it is not an object, adverb or finite verb.
s: Adjective classes, positions and ordered description

q: Choose the ordinary adjective for the affected travellers: The travellers were ____ by the long delay.
e: The travellers experienced exhaustion, so exhausted is the intended participial adjective. Exhausting would characterise something causing exhaustion.
s: Adjective classes, positions and ordered description

q: Which form makes an ordinary comparison with one comparative marker?
e: Colder is comparative and takes than for its standard. The alternatives duplicate degree markers or use a superlative where the stated comparison requires a comparative.
s: Degree, comparison and sense-dependent gradability

q: The revised instructions are ____ clearer than the first draft.
e: Much can modify a comparative. Very clearer is not the ordinary degree pattern; most/more duplicate comparison already marked in clearer.
s: Degree, comparison and sense-dependent gradability

q: Which statement accurately explains “one of the better submissions”?
o: It identifies the single best submission.
It places a submission within a relatively strong group.
It compares a submission with itself.
It is always ungrammatical without best.
e: Better is a legitimate comparative in this expression. It does not force the stronger claim made by best.
s: Degree, comparison and sense-dependent gradability

q: For the intended meaning “with great effort”, choose: The technician worked ____ all afternoon.
e: Hard describes effort. Hardly and hardly ever indicate little activity or low frequency and do not express the stated meaning.
s: Adverb forms, phrases, placement and local scope

q: Which sentence uses an adverb to express the manner of replying?
e: Politely modifies the replying event. Polite is an adjective in the other options.
s: Adverb forms, phrases, placement and local scope

q: Which interpretation follows from “They deliberately did not answer”?
o: Their answer was delayed by weather.
They intended to withhold an answer.
e: Deliberately scopes over not answering, presenting the withholding as intentional. The other interpretations are not supplied by the sentence.
s: Adverb forms, phrases, placement and local scope

q: Which sentence explicitly excludes all other relevant senders?
e: Only directly focuses the subject Maya here. The other options concern added or restricted objects rather than exclusive sender identity.
s: Focus, sentence adverbials and responsible interpretation

q: In standard edited prose, identify the faulty segment or choose No error: (A) The figures were incomplete; (B) nevertheless, (C) the report was useful.
e: The semicolon separates independent clauses; nevertheless marks concession and the comma is appropriate. The sentence needs no correction.
s: Focus, sentence adverbials and responsible interpretation

q: Complete the ordinary temporal expression: The seminar is ____ Tuesday.
e: A named day takes on in this expression. In normally introduces a larger period; at locates a point such as noon.
s: Time, space and abstract relationships

q: Which instruction sets a completion deadline rather than a period of continued waiting?
e: By Friday gives the latest completion time for sending. The other instructions describe continuation.
s: Time, space and abstract relationships

q: Which analysis is correct for “without checking the total”?
e: Checking the total is an -ing clause serving as complement of without.
s: Prepositional phrases, complements and stranding

q: Which statement is accurate?
o: A preposition can never end a standard English sentence.
Which chair did you sit on? is standard preposition stranding.
On which chair did you sit? is always ungrammatical.
All prepositions have exactly one complement type.
e: Stranding is established standard English; pied-piping is also possible. Complement licensing varies lexically.
s: Prepositional phrases, complements and stranding

q: We look forward to ____ the revised draft.
e: To belongs to the lexical expression look forward to and takes an -ing complement here.
s: Lexical selection, fixed combinations and meaning

q: Which sentence uses a grammatical content-clause pattern after insist?
o: She insisted on that the figures were correct.
She insisted to that the figures were correct.
She insisted for that the figures were correct.
She insisted that the figures were correct.
e: Insist may take a content clause directly. Adding on/to/for before this that-clause does not produce the intended pattern.
s: Lexical selection, fixed combinations and meaning

q: Which version uses ordinary personal-pronoun placement with separable turn off?
e: The personal pronoun normally appears between turn and off.
s: Particles, multi-word verbs and cumulative review

q: Which expression is phrasal-prepositional in the narrower three-way classification?
e: Put up with contains verb, particle and preposition. Turn off has a particle; rely on is prepositional in this classification.
s: Particles, multi-word verbs and cumulative review

q: Cumulative review: which sentence explicitly locates an event before a second past event?
o: She has left before the bus arrived.
She had left before the bus arrived.
She will leave before the bus arrived.
She is leaving before the bus arrived.
e: Had left gives the earlier past event in a coherent past narrative. The other tense combinations do not express the stipulated temporal relationship in this context.
s: Past perfect and past perfect progressive: looking back from then

q: Cumulative review, standard edited agreement: (A) The list of revised dates (B) are ready (C) for publication.
e: List is the singular head of the subject, so is ready is required. Revised dates is inside an of-phrase.
s: Person, number and the structure of the subject

q: In “the unusually heavy suitcase”, which word is the noun-phrase head?
e: Suitcase determines the category of the whole noun phrase. Heavy heads an embedded adjective phrase; unusually modifies that adjective.
s: Heads and the central phrase classes

q: Using the narrow verb-group convention taught here, identify the verb group in “They might have missed the train”.
e: The narrow group includes the modal, perfect auxiliary and lexical participle; the object is outside this particular grouping.
s: Heads and the central phrase classes

q: What is the phrase class of “under the stairs” in “The cupboard under the stairs is locked”?
e: Under is the preposition head; the whole phrase postmodifies cupboard. Modifier is its function, not its category.
s: Heads and the central phrase classes

q: Which analysis distinguishes class from function correctly?
o: In “the chair beside the window”, beside the window is a prepositional phrase functioning as postmodifier.
Every modifier must be an adjective.
Every word after a noun is its complement.
A phrase answering where must be an adverb phrase.
e: The phrase is headed by beside and modifies chair from a post-head position. The other claims confuse structure with function.
s: Determiners, modifiers and selected complements

q: Which statement avoids treating optionality as the sole complement test?
o: Every optional expression is an adjunct.
A complement is licensed by its head and may be optional in a given lexical pattern.
Anything after a verb is a complement.
e: Eat licenses an object but can occur without one. Licensing and the particular lexical pattern matter alongside omission.
s: Determiners, modifiers and selected complements

q: Complete standard edited agreement: “The label on the three folders ____ unreadable.”
e: The whole subject is headed by singular label. Folders is embedded inside the on-phrase.
s: Embedding, coordination and structural hierarchy

q: What mainly creates the two familiar readings of “She saw the student with the binoculars”?
o: Different possible attachments of with the binoculars.
e: The phrase can identify the student or describe an instrument used in seeing. Context or explicit restructuring resolves the attachment.
s: Embedding, coordination and structural hierarchy

q: Which conclusion follows from replacing “the revised timetable” with it in “We checked the revised timetable”?
o: The original expression was one pronoun.
The replacement supports the grouping as a noun phrase in that object position.
Every adjacent string can be replaced with it.
The replacement preserves every detail of the original.
e: Substitution supplies evidence for a grouping and position; it does not change the original words’ categories or preserve all descriptive information.
s: Constituency diagnostics and practical parsing

q: Which bracketed analysis locates the adjective phrase correctly?
e: Colleague is a noun head. Very helpful is the adjective phrase modifying it.
s: Constituency diagnostics and practical parsing

q: Assess standard edited grammar: (A) The documents on the shelf (B) are ready (C) for collection.
e: Documents is the plural head of the subject noun phrase and agrees with are. The prepositional phrase does not introduce an agreement fault.
s: Constituency diagnostics and practical parsing

q: Which bracketed unit is a finite subordinate clause in “We waited because the gate was locked”?
e: Because the gate was locked has finite was and is a subordinate reason clause. We waited is the main clause.
s: Main, subordinate, finite and non-finite clauses

q: What is the status of “for the visitors to arrive early” in “For the visitors to arrive early would be convenient”?
o: A non-finite clause functioning as subject
A noun with no clause structure
e: The expressed subject the visitors belongs to a to-infinitival clause. That whole clause functions as subject of would be convenient.
s: Main, subordinate, finite and non-finite clauses

q: How should “Could you close the door?” normally be analysed in a polite request context?
o: A subordinate clause without a main clause
Exclamative form because it is polite
Interrogative form functioning as a request
e: The auxiliary precedes the subject, giving interrogative form; its likely communicative function is requesting action.
s: Clause forms and communicative purposes

q: Which is the neutral subject wh-question?
e: Who is the subject, so the ordinary question does not add do-support before the lexical past form.
s: Clause forms and communicative purposes

q: Which is the central how-exclamative pattern?
e: How carefully she worked has exclamative order. How carefully did she work? is a direct interrogative.
s: Clause forms and communicative purposes

q: Under this lesson’s finite-clause classroom convention, which example clearly has compound architecture?
o: The assistant opened and sorted the post.
The assistant opened the post, and her colleague checked the register.
The assistant opened the post because the manager asked her.
The assistant wanted to sort the post.
e: The keyed sentence has two separately expressed main finite clauses joined by and. The other examples have different architecture under the stated convention.
s: Simple, coordinated and subordinate architecture

q: Which statement describes “She hopes to leave” accurately without hiding a terminology choice?
o: Every grammar must call the sentence simple for the same reason.
There is a main finite clause containing an infinitival complement clause; labels such as complex depend on the stated convention.
There are two independent finite sentences.
To leave cannot be a clause because it has no tense ending.
e: A precise structural description recognises the non-finite complement and allows explicit classification conventions.
s: Simple, coordinated and subordinate architecture

q: Which sentence repairs a fused boundary without adding an unsupported causal or concessive relation?
o: The bell rang; the doors opened.
The bell rang the doors opened.
Because the bell rang. The doors opened.
The bell rang, the doors opened.
e: The semicolon supplies a formal boundary between the related independent clauses without selecting a new causal connector.
s: Clause boundaries and accessible visual parsing

q: In ordinary formal prose, assess: (A) Although the office was closed, (B) the guard accepted the envelope (C) and logged its arrival.
e: The concession clause is attached to a main clause, and the two predicates share the subject the guard. No repair is required.
s: Clause boundaries and accessible visual parsing

q: Why is a comma alone insufficient in “The room was small, however it held everyone” in ordinary formal prose?
o: However is a linking adverb and does not itself coordinate the independent clauses.
The second clause contains no finite verb.
e: A semicolon or full stop should provide the boundary before however; held is a finite verb and the other suggested faults are not present.
s: Clause boundaries and accessible visual parsing

q: The intended meaning singles out online applicants from a larger group. Which version marks an integrated defining relative?
o: The applicants who registered online received a link.
The applicants, that registered online, received a link.
The applicants, received a link who registered online.
The applicants, who registered online, received a link.
e: The unpunctuated who-clause identifies the relevant subset. The comma-marked version instead presents supplementary information about already identified applicants.
s: Defining and supplementary relative information

q: Which marker is licensed in the ordinary supplementary relative: “The library, ____ roof was damaged, is closed”?
e: Whose expresses the genitive relation to roof and can have a non-human antecedent such as library.
s: Defining and supplementary relative information

q: Which statement accurately describes British English relative usage?
o: Object who is ungrammatical in all registers.
That must follow a fronted preposition.
Defining which is grammatical, though some editorial styles prefer that.
Which is never allowed in a defining relative.
e: The British pattern permits restrictive which. The other claims falsely turn a style or register preference into a universal rule.
s: Defining and supplementary relative information

q: Which sentence contains an ordinary integrated contact relative?
o: The file, I requested, has arrived.
The file arrived yesterday has been approved, intending file as the subject of arrived within a relative.
The file, that I requested, has arrived.
The file I requested has arrived.
e: I requested is an integrated object relative with no overt marker. Supplementary relatives and ordinary finite subject relatives do not allow that same deletion pattern.
s: Contact clauses and non-finite relatives

q: Which analysis of “the forms received yesterday” fits the ordinary intended reading?
o: A finite active relative with subject forms.
A non-finite participial postmodifier with a passive interpretation.
e: Received yesterday is a past-participial non-finite modifier; it does not independently mark finite past tense or future perfect aspect.
s: Contact clauses and non-finite relatives

q: In “the claim that the manager resigned”, how does the that-clause function?
o: It supplies the content of the claim.
It is an adjective word rather than a clause.
It is a relative with an object gap after resigned.
e: The clause the manager resigned is internally complete and states the content of the claim. There is no object gap linked to claim.
s: Content, nominal and embedded interrogative structures

q: Complete the standard non-finite embedded-question pattern: “She is deciding ____ to accept the offer.”
e: Whether introduces an alternative before the to-infinitive. If to accept is not the corresponding standard pattern.
s: Content, nominal and embedded interrogative structures

q: Which version has ordinary embedded-question order?
o: We know where does the archive be.
We know that where the archive is.
We know where the archive is.
We know where is the archive.
e: The embedded question keeps subject the archive before is. No additional that belongs before where in this intended pattern.
s: Content, nominal and embedded interrogative structures

q: Which sentence explicitly expresses an intended purpose?
o: We left early so that we could catch the shuttle.
We left when the bell rang.
We left although the discussion continued.
We left because the hall was closing.
e: So that we could catch the shuttle states the intended goal. The other clauses express reason, time and concession respectively.
s: Adverbial clauses and semantic relationships

q: Assess standard edited grammar: (A) Although the room was small, (B) the volunteers arranged the chairs (C) so that everyone could see the screen.
e: The concession clause is attached to its main clause and the purpose clause has a clear subject and modal pattern. No correction is required.
s: Adverbial clauses and semantic relationships

q: In “The room was quiet and without windows”, what functions do the coordinated phrases share?
e: Quiet is an adjective phrase and without windows a prepositional phrase; both describe the subject predicatively. They are not objects or clauses.
s: Coordination and subordination: what is connected

q: Which example coordinates two complete clauses with separate overt subjects?
o: Mina checked the forms and Omar stamped them.
Mina and Omar checked the forms.
Mina checked and stamped the forms.
e: In the correct sentence Mina is the subject of checked and Omar is the subject of stamped, so each coordinated clause has its own overt subject and finite predicate.
s: Coordination and subordination: what is connected

q: Both the label and the separate seal ____ missing. Choose agreement for the two-item subject.
e: Two separate singular items joined by both…and form a plural subject; are supplies the plural finite verb.
s: Correlative patterns, agreement and balanced alternatives

q: Which sentence denies that either of the two applications was approved?
e: Neither excludes approval of each application. Not both allows one approval.
s: Correlative patterns, agreement and balanced alternatives

q: Choose the standard inversion after clause-initial not only.
o: Not only did finished the team early.
Not only the team finished did early.
Not only the team did finish early.
Not only did the team finish early.
e: The auxiliary did precedes the subject, and finish remains base form.
s: Correlative patterns, agreement and balanced alternatives

q: Complete the stated reason: “We postponed the trip ____ the bridge was closed.”
e: The following finite clause needs because for the requested reason; the other options do not take that complement in this pattern.
s: Logic: addition, contrast, concession and qualification

q: Which connector explicitly presents a contrary-to-expectation relation?
o: Before the room was small, everyone found a seat.
If the room was small, everyone found a seat.
Although the room was small, everyone found a seat.
Because the room was small, everyone found a seat.
e: Although marks concession. Because asserts a reason, before time, and if a condition.
s: Logic: addition, contrast, concession and qualification

q: Express purpose with the finite clause shown: “We lowered the screen ____ children could see it.”
e: So that introduces the stated finite purpose clause. The infinitival expressions require a base verb rather than children could.
s: Logic: addition, contrast, concession and qualification

q: Identify the fault in edited prose: “The queue grew, however the gate stayed shut.”
o: The independent clauses need an appropriate boundary.
e: The comma alone does not connect independent clauses with however. A full stop or semicolon repairs the boundary.
s: Connector classes and punctuation in use

q: Assess: “The report was brief; however, it addressed every objection.”
e: The semicolon separates independent clauses and however marks the contrast. Brief is a predicative adjective and every selects singular objection.
s: Connector classes and punctuation in use

q: Choose the core-modal verb chain: “She might ____ arrived.”
e: The first verb after might takes base form have; perfect have then takes arrived.
s: Core modals, marginal forms and substitutes

q: Which question uses core must without unnecessary do-support?
e: Core must forms the interrogative by inversion.
s: Core modals, marginal forms and substitutes

q: Choose an infinitival expression of ability after want.
o: I want to can read it.
I want can to read it.
I want to be able to read it.
I want to could read it.
e: Core can has no ordinary to-infinitive; be able to supplies the required form.
s: Core modals, marginal forms and substitutes

q: A notice means entry is forbidden. Which wording preserves that meaning?
o: You do not have to enter.
e: Must not prohibits entry; the other wordings allow a choice or remove obligation.
s: Ability, permission, necessity and inference

q: In “Her car is outside; she must be home”, must primarily expresses:
o: An order for her to go home
e: The evidence supports a deduction about location rather than a directive.
s: Ability, permission, necessity and inference

q: In “Would you close the window, please?”, the usual communicative function is:
o: A report of a past habit
A claim that closing is impossible
e: The interrogative conventionally requests action; it need not test ability literally.
s: Ability, permission, necessity and inference

q: The waiting happened but was unnecessary: “You ____ waited; I had my own key.” Choose the construction that explicitly carries that reading.
o: did not need to have to
e: Need not have + participle presents the waiting as actual and unnecessary.
s: Modal perfects: evidence, regret and unnecessary actions

q: Which statement is accurate about “We did not need to pay”?
o: It entails that we did not pay.
It states absence of necessity but leaves performance open.
e: Non-payment may be suggested in conversation, but the sentence can be followed by but we paid anyway.
s: Modal perfects: evidence, regret and unnecessary actions

q: Assess the verb chain: “She should have wrote the address.”
e: Perfect have requires the past participle written.
s: Modal perfects: evidence, regret and unnecessary actions

q: Which version limits its claim to the evidence of a small pilot?
o: The pilot proves no study is needed.
The treatment always works for everyone.
The pilot suggests a possible benefit in the sampled group.
e: The version referring to a possible benefit preserves uncertainty and limits the population instead of generalising beyond the stated evidence.
s: Epistemic and deontic meaning, hedging and commitment

q: Which sentence presents an open future condition rather than a remote alternative?
o: If the printer worked now, we would use it.
If the printer had worked yesterday, we would have used it.
If the printer had worked yesterday, we would be finished now.
If the printer works tomorrow, we will use it.
e: The present if-clause with tomorrow leaves a future possibility open; the other choices explicitly present remote alternatives.
s: Conditional meaning: patterns, reality and time

q: The key was not brought, and entry was impossible yesterday. Which sentence imagines that different past?
o: If we had brought the key, we could have entered.
If we bring the key, we entered.
If we had bringing the key, we could enter.
If we bring the key, we can enter.
e: Had brought plus could have entered expresses the earlier counterfactual situation; the first is open future/present, and the others do not form the intended verb chains.
s: Conditional meaning: patterns, reality and time

q: Choose the accurate analysis of “If she will wait, I can explain”. Here will means willingness.
o: Will legitimately expresses willingness in this if-clause.
Can must be replaced by will in every result clause.
Will is automatically wrong after if.
The sentence must refer to yesterday.
e: Modal willingness is an established exception to the simplified future-clause rule.
s: Conditional meaning: patterns, reality and time

q: Express a regret about an omission yesterday: “I wish I ____ the serial number yesterday.”
e: Had noted supplies the past-perfect form for an earlier regret.
s: Wishes, regrets, preferences and apparent situations

q: Which construction expresses a present preference about another person’s action?
o: I would rather you has wait outside.
I would rather you waited outside.
I would rather to you wait outside.
I would rather you to waiting outside.
e: Would rather plus a different subject can take a past clause for a present or future preference.
s: Wishes, regrets, preferences and apparent situations

q: Complete the formal inversion: “Had I ____ the notice, I would have replied.”
e: Auxiliary had takes the participle seen, not past simple saw.
s: Formal conditional inversion and conditional links

q: Which is the formal conditional counterpart of “If you should need a copy, contact reception”?
o: Should you need a copy, contact reception.
If should you need a copy, contact reception.
Need you should a copy, contact reception.
Should you needed a copy, contact reception.
e: Should precedes the subject, if is omitted, and need remains a base form.
s: Formal conditional inversion and conditional links

q: A formal British report says “They recommended that the hearing should be postponed.” What is defensible?
o: Should must always be deleted as ungrammatical.
Recommended can never introduce a that-clause.
The hearing must take a plural verb.
Should be is a legitimate mandative alternative.
e: British English accepts mandative should; the plain-form be alternative is also standard.
s: Mood, mandative meaning and cumulative analysis

q: Inspect the verb chain: “The policy requires that each visitor be registered.”
o: be must become is in every context
e: Plain be is standard in a mandative clause; singular each visitor does not require is in that construction.
s: Mood, mandative meaning and cumulative analysis

q: In “She insisted that she was innocent”, the supplied context is an assertion, not a demand. Which analysis fits?
o: The content clause has no subject.
An indicative content clause reports her assertion.
Was must become be merely because insist occurs.
Insist must be followed by on here.
e: Insist can report an emphatic assertion with an indicative that-clause; it does not always select on or a mandative.
s: Mood, mandative meaning and cumulative analysis

q: Keep the ongoing present reading: “The technician is repairing the scanner” → “The scanner ____ by the technician.”
e: Is being repaired preserves present progressive aspect and changes voice.
s: Building the passive verb phrase

q: Complete the perfect passive: “The letters have been ____.”
e: Passive be requires the lexical participle written.
s: Building the passive verb phrase

q: Which sequence is a passive infinitive?
e: To be checked contains infinitival be plus the lexical participle.
s: Building the passive verb phrase

q: A report says “The manuscript is believed to have survived the fire.” What does that form establish?
o: Survival is attributed as a belief, with earlier time reference.
The sentence proves survival beyond doubt.
The fire will necessarily occur tomorrow.
Believed must be replaced by believing.
e: The construction reports a belief and uses the perfect infinitive for an earlier event; attribution is not proof.
s: Agents, reporting, get-passives and two-object verbs

q: Which statement about “She got promoted” is accurate?
o: Got promoted is automatically an adjective before a noun.
Get-passives can describe a positive event.
e: Get-passives are not confined to undesirable outcomes and do not by themselves assign blame.
s: Agents, reporting, get-passives and two-object verbs

q: Use active causative make: “The interruption made us ____ again.”
e: Active causative make selects object plus bare infinitive start.
s: Causatives and their complement patterns

q: Which pair consists of two standard help constructions?
o: help me checks / help me checking
help me check / help me to check
help me checking / help me checked
help to me check / help me to checking
e: Help accepts an object followed by an infinitive with or without to.
s: Causatives and their complement patterns

q: Inspect: “The visitors were made to wait outside.”
o: to must be deleted after passive made
e: Passive made takes to wait; plural visitors agrees with were.
s: Causatives and their complement patterns

q: Which sentence contains an established prepositional passive?
o: The visitor was became a member.
e: Look into permits this prepositional passive; the other verbs do not form the proposed passives in these uses.
s: Passivisation limits, ergative alternation and meaning

q: In “The ice melted”, which analysis is correct?
o: Passive solely because ice is affected
Passive perfect because melted ends in -ed
A causative clause with an expressed agent
e: The clause has an active intransitive verb; an affected subject alone does not establish passive voice.
s: Passivisation limits, ergative alternation and meaning

q: In The archivist hopes to finish today, which expression is the non-finite complement?
e: To finish today is an infinitival clause complement. Hopes is the finite matrix verb; today alone is only an adverbial expression.
s: Non-finite forms and grammatical functions

q: Complete the perfect passive infinitive: The letter appears to have been ____.
e: Have been written is a perfect passive chain ending in the lexical participle written.
s: Non-finite forms and grammatical functions

q: Which analysis distinguishes a verbal -ing clause from a noun phrase?
o: Carefully is an adjective modifying a noun in reading the files carefully.
Reading the files carefully contains a verbal reading with an object and adverb.
The careful reading of the files must contain a finite verb.
Every spelling ending in -ing is automatically a verb.
e: The direct object the files and adverb carefully support a verbal analysis. A noun reading instead permits determiner/adjective and an of-phrase.
s: Non-finite forms and grammatical functions

q: We look forward to ____ the new curator.
e: In look forward to, to is prepositional and the following activity complement uses -ing.
s: Verb complementation and differences in meaning

q: Mina stopped to read the notice. What does the infinitive normally express?
o: Proof that the notice was never read
The ending of the reading activity
The purpose of pausing another activity
e: Stopped to read normally means paused in order to read; stopped reading would mean ceased reading.
s: Verb complementation and differences in meaning

q: Review: They helped us to carry the boxes.
o: Helped must always be followed by an -ing form.
To must be removed because help never allows it.
Us must be replaced by we.
No error: help permits an infinitive with or without to.
e: Help us carry and help us to carry are both standard; the object pronoun us is appropriate.
s: Verb complementation and differences in meaning

q: The intended inspector is Samir. Which revision clearly supplies that participant?
o: After the roof inspected Samir, the leak was obvious.
Having inspected the roof, the leak was obvious.
After Samir inspected the roof, the leak was obvious to him.
Having inspected the roof, the leak inspected Samir.
e: The finite after-clause explicitly identifies Samir as inspector while preserving that he found the leak obvious.
s: Purpose, participial clauses and meaning-preserving reduction

q: Which opening clause has its own expressed subject rather than an ordinary shared main-clause subject?
o: Warned about the closure, Nora stayed.
Having checked the list, Nora called.
To check the list, Nora stayed.
e: Weather permitting is an absolute construction with weather as its own subject. The other examples have an understood participant linked to Nora.
s: Purpose, participial clauses and meaning-preserving reduction

q: In Amina persuaded Omar to attend, who is the understood attendee in the ordinary intended reading?
e: Persuade licenses object/goal control: Omar is the intended attendee, while Amina is the persuader.
s: Control, raising and the interpretation of non-finite subjects

q: Which example supports a raising analysis of seem rather than an agentive subject-control analysis?
o: There seems to be a delay.
The technician tried to restart the machine.
The supervisor persuaded us to stay.
The guide asked us to wait.
e: Dummy there can occur with seems to be without naming an agent of seem. Try, persuade and ask in the other examples involve participant/control relationships.
s: Control, raising and the interpretation of non-finite subjects

q: Which unquoted report has ordinary embedded-question order?
o: She asked where did the keys be.
She asked where the keys were.
She asked where were the keys.
She asked that where the keys were.
e: An embedded non-subject wh-question uses subject–verb order; where does not combine with that here.
s: Reported questions and embedded interrogatives

q: Use standard reported-request grammar: The steward asked us ____.
e: Ask + recipient + to-infinitive reports this request; a bare form or gerund does not fill that pattern.
s: Commands, requests and reporting-verb patterns

q: A Wednesday report describes a gate that reopened on Tuesday. On Monday the guard said that the gate ____ .
e: Was closed adopts Monday’s viewpoint; is closed now would incorrectly assert current closure.
s: Backshift and temporal relationships

q: Choose the genuine error in formal edited English: “She asked whether to wait and I wondered where the exit was.”
e: Whether can introduce a to-infinitive and the embedded wh-clause has ordinary order.
s: Reported questions and embedded interrogatives

q: Which sentence reports a suggestion using a standard complement pattern?
o: He suggested to us that we return.
e: Suggest can take a that-clause and a to-phrase addressee; the alternatives mix incompatible patterns.
s: Commands, requests and reporting-verb patterns

q: Which form places the warning against disclosure inside the reported instruction?
o: She warned not us disclose it.
She warned us to not it disclose.
She did not warn us to disclose it.
She warned us not to disclose it.
e: Not to disclose is the prohibited action; did not warn denies the act of warning.
s: Commands, requests and reporting-verb patterns

q: The original speaker and reporter are both me. Which report preserves that identity?
o: I said that I was ready.
I said that myself was ready.
I said that she was ready, meaning myself.
I said that they were me ready.
e: Self-report can keep I; an automatic I→he/she replacement would change reference.
s: Quoting, reporting and choosing a perspective

q: Which full sentence requires a question mark?
o: She asked where the archive was
I wondered whether the archive was open
Do you know whether the archive is open
The notice explains when the archive opens
e: The outer clause Do you know ...? asks a direct question; its embedded clause keeps statement order.
s: Reported questions and embedded interrogatives

q: Which claim about backshift is accurate?
o: Was in a report proves the state has ended.
Every past report must change every tense.
A past report can retain present tense for a still-current fact.
Past perfect must become a new earlier tense.
e: Backshift reflects viewpoint; continuing truth can justify present tense, and a shifted past need not imply cessation.
s: Backshift and temporal relationships

q: Which reporting verb normally asserts successful influence?
e: Persuaded someone to do something normally entails successful influence; advice and suggestions need not be followed.
s: Commands, requests and reporting-verb patterns

q: Who is understood to be carrying the parcels in “Carrying two parcels, Asha rang the bell”?
e: The ordinary subjectless participial adjunct shares its understood participant with main subject Asha.
s: Placing modifiers and recovering their subjects

q: The intended carrier was the courier, not the parcel. Which rewrite expresses that?
o: The courier was entered by the carrying parcel.
Carrying a parcel, the courier entered.
Carrying a courier, the parcel entered.
The parcel, carrying a courier, entered.
e: The main subject courier is a suitable understood carrier; the other versions reverse roles.
s: Placing modifiers and recovering their subjects

q: Which statement means at least some claims were not approved, without saying none were approved?
o: Not all the claims were approved.
None of the claims was approved.
e: Not all denies universal approval; none and no deny all approval, and every asserts it.
s: Attachment, scope and reference

q: Find the fault, if any: “Damaged in transit, the instruments were returned.”
e: The instruments are both what were damaged and what were returned; passive main voice does not create a dangling modifier.
s: Placing modifiers and recovering their subjects

q: Choose a complement pattern allowed by enjoy.
o: She enjoys drafting and to edit.
She enjoys to draft and editing.
e: Enjoy selects the relevant -ing complements; the coordination must fit that head.
s: Parallelism, correlatives and comparisons

q: For the explicit intended comparison of salaries, which sentence is clearest?
o: Her salary is higher her assistant.
Her assistant is higher salary than her.
Her salary is higher than her assistant.
Her salary is higher than her assistant’s salary.
e: The second version explicitly compares salary with salary, preserving the stated intention.
s: Predication and meaning-preserving revision

q: Which revision preserves “They decided to postpone the visit” without asserting the visit was postponed?
o: They reached a decision to postpone the visit.
e: Reached a decision preserves the decision; implementation or cancellation is not entailed.
s: Predication and meaning-preserving revision

q: In which example does This refer to the preceding event rather than identify or modify an object?
o: This is the notebook Nora lent me.
Please put this beside the other notebook.
The server failed. This interrupted the booking service.
e: In the server example, This refers to the event of failure. In the other examples it modifies or identifies a concrete object in context.
s: Attachment, scope and reference

q: Identify the genuine error in “The position involves checking invoices, filing receipts and to answer calls.”
e: The final to-infinitive does not fit the complements selected by involves here; answering calls fits.
s: Parallelism, correlatives and comparisons

q: Which initial construction supplies its own explicit subject?
e: The meeting finished is an absolute construction; meeting is its own explicit subject.
s: Placing modifiers and recovering their subjects

q: Complete the formal negative-fronting pattern: Never ____ this route before.
e: Never as a fronted negative adjunct triggers subject–auxiliary inversion: have we used.
s: Negative, concessive and conditional inversion

q: Which sentence has a negative subject with ordinary order?
e: Nobody is the subject; a negative subject does not require inversion, and did would take a bare verb.
s: Negative, concessive and conditional inversion

q: Choose a formal inverted conditional equivalent to If we had noticed, we would have stopped.
o: Had we noticed, we would have stopped.
Did we had noticed, we would have stopped.
Had noticed we if, we would have stopped.
If had we noticed, we would have stopped.
e: Had + subject + participle replaces this if-clause; do not retain if.
s: Negative, concessive and conditional inversion

q: Find a genuine fault, if any: “Only Mira knew the password.”
e: Only modifies the subject; ordinary subject–verb order is appropriate.
s: Negative, concessive and conditional inversion

q: Which it-cleft retains singular initial it with a plural focus?
o: It was the porters who finds the crate.
It are the porters who found the crate.
It were the porters who found the crate.
It was the porters who found the crate.
e: Initial it takes was; the cleft clause’s plural porters takes found, whose past form is number-neutral.
s: Fronting, clefts and organising focus

q: What does it do in It is surprising that nobody called?
o: Refers to a previously named caller.
e: It supports an extraposed content clause and has no ordinary referent.
s: Extraposition, existential presentation and end-weight

q: Use formal edited agreement: There ____ two unclaimed packages.
e: The formal plural presentational pattern uses are with packages; informal there’s plural is a separate usage.
s: Extraposition, existential presentation and end-weight

q: Which form correctly uses emphatic do?
e: Does is finite and carries agreement; remember remains a bare form.
s: Emphatic auxiliaries, substitution and ellipsis

q: Complete a matching perfect elliptical answer: Has the alarm been tested? Yes, it ____.
e: Has retains the perfect auxiliary; been tested is understood.
s: Emphatic auxiliaries, substitution and ellipsis

q: Which analysis is accurate for Exhausted though he was, he continued?
o: The adjective is fronted in a concessive construction.
He was must become was he.
The word exhausted must be an adverb.
e: Concessive fronting differs from subject–auxiliary inversion and keeps he was here.
s: Negative, concessive and conditional inversion

q: Which version is a complete, correctly punctuated sentence in formal edited prose?
e: A semicolon links two independent clauses; the other options contain a comma splice, subordinate fragment or fused boundary.
s: Clause boundaries, commas and semicolons

q: The introductory clause gives a reason. Choose the clear standard punctuation.
o: Because the road was closed; we turned back.
Because, the road was closed we turned back.
Because the road was closed, we turned back.
Because the road, was closed we turned back.
e: The comma separates a complete opening reason clause from its main clause; the semicolon cannot make the subordinate clause independent.
s: Clause boundaries, commas and semicolons

q: Which form means a lounge used by several teachers?
e: The regular plural teachers takes its possessive apostrophe after s; lounge is singular.
s: Colons, apostrophes and compact written forms

q: Choose the genuine error in this sentence: Its clear that the team retained its records.
e: The opening needs It’s, meaning it is. The later possessive its is correct.
s: Colons, apostrophes and compact written forms

q: Which sentence itself asks a question?
o: Do you know whether the gate was open?
I wondered whether the gate was open.
She asked whether the gate was open.
The question is whether the gate was open.
e: Only Do you know ...? is an outer interrogative. All embedded clauses retain statement-like subject–verb order.
s: Quotation, interruption and sentence-final marks

q: Which is a correctly formed compound premodifier?
e: A numerical unit in this compound premodifier uses singular year and a hyphen; the distractors mix plural or possessive structures.
s: Quotation, interruption and sentence-final marks

q: Which statement about quotation styles is accurate?
o: Nested quotation marks can never be used.
Only double outer quotation marks are grammatical.
Only single outer quotation marks are grammatical.
Single or double outer marks can follow established style conventions.
e: Established styles differ; the chosen outer/inner system should keep quotation levels clear.
s: Quotation, interruption and sentence-final marks

q: Which is a standard American alternative to the British spelling colour?
e: Color is the established American form. The other options are not the standard alternatives.
s: Capitalisation, spelling and editorial consistency

q: Choose the genuine error: The report—after several revisions—was approved.
e: The paired dashes enclose an aside and the remaining clause is complete; no repair is required.
s: Quotation, interruption and sentence-final marks

q: What is the strongest reason not to remove not from a quotation while using an ellipsis?
o: The omission reverses the represented meaning.
An ellipsis can never omit any word.
e: Ellipses may indicate omissions, but the resulting quotation must represent the source faithfully.
s: Quotation, interruption and sentence-final marks

q: Choose the word meaning give a recommendation: Please ____ the new staff about the procedure.
e: Advise is the verb required after imperative please; advice is the related noun.
s: Confusable words: meaning before substitution

q: Which sentence uses effect as a standard verb meaning bring about?
o: The effect of the agreement was small.
e: Effected means brought about; the other uses are nouns. Effect is not restricted to noun use.
s: Confusable words: meaning before substitution

q: Which adjective means relating to courts, without saying a decision was wise?
e: Judicial identifies a legal/court relationship; judicious evaluates sound judgement.
s: Confusable words: meaning before substitution

q: Choose the genuine error: We discussed about the revised budget.
e: For the intended ordinary transitive discuss pattern, remove about. The noun discussion can take about.
s: Lexical patterns and preposition choices

q: Which statement about insist is accurate?
o: It takes only an infinitive with no subject.
It must always be followed immediately by on.
It can take on + noun/-ing or a that-clause.
It can never express a demand.
e: Both insist on checking and insist that we check are standard patterns.
s: Lexical patterns and preposition choices

q: Which expression identifies the SIZE of a rise, rather than what rises?
o: an increase of six per cent
e: Of six per cent measures the amount; in + variable identifies what changes.
s: Lexical patterns and preposition choices

q: Which is standard ordinary usage?
e: Advice is uncountable in the intended ordinary sense; pieces supplies countable units.
s: Countability, agreement and national alternatives

q: Choose the genuine error in formal British English: The committee are divided in their views.
e: British member-oriented collective agreement can be plural; the supplied context makes it appropriate.
s: Countability, agreement and national alternatives

q: Which judgement about prepone is defensible?
o: It is recorded in Indian English; bring forward may be clearer to unfamiliar readers.
It is a mandatory international form.
It is not an English word in any variety.
e: The dictionary records regional use. Audience-based paraphrase is distinct from a universal error judgement.
s: Register, regional English and evidence-based editing

q: Which correction repairs a genuine auxiliary-pattern error?
o: committee are → committee is in every British context
insure → ensure in every American context
e: The present perfect requires the participle gone. The other changes depend on region, register or interpretation.
s: Register, regional English and evidence-based editing

q: What does it refer to in A parcel arrived. It was empty?
e: It continues the established parcel noun phrase.
s: Connecting sentences: cohesion, reference and recoverable omission

q: Choose the meaningful substitute: She promised to inspect the valve and ____.
e: Did so substitutes for the inspection action; one would substitute for a noun.
s: Connecting sentences: cohesion, reference and recoverable omission

q: Identify the genuine error: The ferry arrived yesterday. It carries passengers daily.
e: The past arrival event and present habitual service justify different tenses.
s: Time, topics and the movement of information

q: Which relation does nevertheless normally signal?
e: Nevertheless presents a contrasting outcome that holds despite an expectation.
s: Time, topics and the movement of information

q: All six interviewees expressed support. These interviews are the only evidence supplied. Which statement is appropriately limited to that evidence?
e: The answer reports the observed group; the other claims extend beyond the supplied evidence.
s: Academic compression, hedging and economical variety

q: Which is an example of nominalisation?
e: Approval packages the event as a noun; the other options use verb approve.
s: Academic compression, hedging and economical variety

q: After The report and the map were missing, which continuation explicitly identifies the map?
e: Repeating map removes competition between two singular referents.
s: Connecting sentences: cohesion, reference and recoverable omission

q: Which is true of cohesion and coherence?
o: Coherence requires the same tense everywhere.
Every this must precede a noun.
A connector guarantees a valid argument.
Cohesive links can exist in an incoherent argument.
e: Visible links do not establish logical sense or truth; tense and reference remain contextual.
s: Connecting sentences: cohesion, reference and recoverable omission

q: Which sentence explicitly retains possibility?
o: The measure certainly caused the change.
The measure must have caused the change.
The measure may have caused the change.
e: May have caused expresses possibility rather than certainty or a strong deduction.
s: Academic compression, hedging and economical variety

q: Choose the genuine error in this formal passage: The first lease expired; the second did not.
e: The omitted expire is recoverable after did not; the passage is grammatical.
s: Connecting sentences: cohesion, reference and recoverable omission

q: Which statement preserves a decision without asserting that it was carried out?
